title: The evolution of elasmobranch assessment and management with data-limited dilemmas

authors.affiliation: Centre for Environment, Fisheries & Aquaculture Science (Cefas), Lowestoft
Centre for Environment, Fisheries & Aquaculture Science (Cefas), Lowestoft

abstract_text: Elasmobranchs in the North-east Atlantic have been exploited for several hundred years, with historical fisheries targeting Basking Shark, skates, Spurdog and Porbeagle. Despite the well-documented vulnerability of elasmobranch fish to over-exploitation, fisheries assessment and management in European waters focused initially on teleosts. European fisheries management measures for fisheries taking elasmobranchs have been introduced since the 1990s, but only became restrictive in the last decade. Current management measures include quota management (e.g. for skates) and prohibited listings for threatened species (e.g. Angelshark). The International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) Working Group on Elasmobranch Fishes are tasked with assessing 55 elasmobranch stocks for ICES advice. There is one benchmarked assessment (Spurdog), and data-limited approaches are used to assess other stocks. These methods include using fisheries-independent survey indices that provide long-term, species-specific data on relative abundance, trends in landings data, or methods incorporating life-history data (e.g. changes in length composition of catches). ICES is now developing alternative data-limited assessment methods that will hopefully translate into more robust assessments in the future, especially for skates, and inform on pragmatic and biologically meaningful management measures for stocks currently unmanaged (e.g. smooth-hounds). Whilst Europe's most depleted elasmobranch species remain scarce, several species are showing recent positive trends in stock status, suggesting the reductions in fishing effort by European fleets are allowing elasmobranch populations to recover. The gradual evolution of elasmobranch fisheries science, assessment and management are described, highlighting progress to date, and identifying ongoing and emerging issues still to be addressed.

title: New frontiers - collaborative partnerships to reduce Spurdog by-catch and dead discards

abstract_text: Spurdog Squalus acanthias L. in the North-east Atlantic is classed as endangered by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and is managed under a zero Total Allowable Catch (TAC), whereby no landings are allowed by European Union (EU) Member State countries. A zero TAC leads to zero landings, but not a zero take from the stock as incidental by-catch of Spurdog can occur in mixed fisheries, leading to fishing induced mortality and wasteful dead discards. Under the reformed Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), implementation of a discard ban with a zero TAC has the potential for Spurdog to become a choke species in mixed fisheries, forcing fishermen to stop fishing and tie-up their vessels in port where Spurdog are caught as by-catch. A collaborative research partnership between Government policy advisors, Government scientists, the fishing industry and an environmental non-governmental organisation (ENGO) has provided a better understanding of Spurdog seasonal spatial movements, vertical behaviour and discard survival and informed the development of a by-catch avoidance programme. In its trial stage, fishermen make informed decisions on their fishing behaviours, avoiding Spurdog aggregations and possibly moving to less productive fishing grounds. To offset any economic disincentive, the provision of a marketable dead Spurdog by-catch allowance has recently been secured through engagement with the European Commission. This evidence based approach will promote Spurdog by-catch avoidance, reduce overall fishing mortality, enable stock recovery, minimise the risk of creating a choke species and end the practice of wasteful dead discarding.

title: Supporting sustainable fisheries for sharks, skates and rays: a Shark Trust perspective
abstract_text: A key conservation aim for the Shark Trust is the sustainable management of non-threatened elasmobranch populations and their associated fisheries. To achieve this, the Trust is clearly supporting certain fisheries shown to be sustainable, while continuing to advocate for effective protection and management of threatened species. At present the Trust is involved in three such projects: In the Southwest of England the Shark Trust is working with the catching sector, processors and national supermarket chains to assess the sustainability of certain UK regional skate and ray fisheries. For those fisheries demonstrated to be sustainable, Shark Trust Sustainable Sourcing Guides – aimed at seafood retailers – will underpin confidence in the sale of selected, appropriately managed species. The Shark Trust is a partner in the Spurdog By-catch Avoidance Programme, which will operate off the Southwest of England. The objective of the programme is to reduce by-catch mortality through utilisation by participating vessels of a real-time by-catch avoidance tool; participating vessels will also have access to a limited by-catch allowance permitting landing and sale of dead Spurdog Squalus acanthias, with full traceability integrated into the supply chain. The Shark Trust is in the preliminary stages of a project working with the Falkland Islands Fisheries Department (FID) to improve recording and reporting in Falkland skate fisheries. At present all skate landings are aggregated; the Trust is working with FID in development of multi-language, species-specific ID materials to improve the quality of catch and landing data, feeding into more effective management of skate stocks.

title: Temperature preference and thermal niche of the southern stingray Dasyatis americana in The Bahamas

authors.affiliation: Newcastle University and The Cape Eleuthera Institute
Newcastle University and The Cape Eleuthera Institute
Newcastle University and The Cape Eleuthera Institute

abstract_text: Temperature is a key factor influencing physiology and behaviour of marine species, particularly ectotherms. In order to optimise physiological processes, such as growth, digestion or metabolic rate, ectotherms must vary body temperatures through behavioural thermoregulation, ultimately leading to changes in movement and utilisation of habitat. Within a population it would therefore be expected that differences in life history trade-offs between individuals may lead to differences in temperature utilisation. Although this has been shown consistently within laboratory experiments there is little evidence of such differences in temperature preference impacting habitat utilisation in the field and even less for elasmobranch fishes. This study aimed to investigate whether differences in life-history stage and sex led to differences in thermal niche within a sub-population of Southern Stingrays, Dasyatis americana, located in the coastal waters of Cape Eleuthera, The Bahamas. A total of 38 temperature loggers were attached to southern stingrays in three groups (mature males, mature females and immature females). In addition environmental loggers were placed at capture locations to compare thermal niche of stingrays to ambient temperatures. To date a total of 11 temperature loggers have been retrieved from stingrays. Preliminary analysis has revealed significant differences in median temperatures stingrays experience with two distinct groups seen. Differences are not explained by location of stingray tagged or date tagged deployed. A Principle Component of Neighbourhood Matrices (PCNM) will be conducted to analyse differences in temperature time series for individual rays. Understanding within population variation in the impact of abiotic factors on movement and habitat use is key to develop future conservation and management programmes for ecological important species.

title: Intertidal feeding of rays – are all sandflats created equal?
abstract_text: An important aspect of the conservation of any species is undeniably knowledge of their habitat preference and patterns of behaviour. In New Zealand, as with all other countries, increasing urbanisation and industrialisation of coastal areas and the increase in terrestrially sourced sedimentation in estuarine environments is resulting in ecological changes and loss of biodiversity in the marine environment. Intertidal sandflats provide the New Zealand Eagle Ray Myliobatis tenuicaudatus an important foraging environment where the evidence of their feeding is apparent by the presence of distinct excavations. As part of a larger study on human influences on ray use of the Tauranga Harbour, New Zealand, these excavations are being used in order to quantify feeding effort in a number of intertidal sandflat areas of similar bathymetric heights to identify any patterns. Small scale patchiness of M. tenuicaudatus feeding pit density has previously been found to be non-linearly related to densities of one prey species. However, it is unknown whether this relationship is consistent over larger geographic areas and particularly across sites with different biophysical characteristics. Preliminary data presented here shows a marked difference in pit density between sites, suggesting that all sandflats are not created equal, and the impact of sedimentation on the structure of the infaunal assemblages may be influencing the feeding effort of rays.

title: Biological observations and spatio-temporal movements of the Common Skate Dipturus batis complex in the Celtic Sea

abstract_text: Since the second half of the 20th century, the Common Skate complex (Dipturus batis and D. cf. intermedia) have undergone severe contractions in their distributions in the North-east Atlantic, presumably in relation to over-fishing. This decline led to 'Common Skate' being listed as 'Critically Endangered' by the IUCN, and the Common Skate complex have been removed from EU fishing opportunities since 2009, with them listed as 'prohibited species' since 2010. In this study, the results of a five-year tagging programme (August 2011 – September 2015) investigating the spatial and temporal movements of 'Common Skate' in the Celtic Sea are presented. In all, 2,071 'Common Skate' (2,017 D. batis and 49 D. cf. intermedia) were recorded, tagged and released with mark-identification tags, of which 25 (1.2%) have been returned. Additionally, 54 specimens (40 D. batis and 14 D. cf. intermedia) were tagged with floated archival tags to collect higher resolution data (depth and temperature records at 10 minute intervals throughout their time at liberty). Ten (20%) of these archival tags have been returned, yielding over 1,500 days of finer-scale data on their vertical and spatial movements. From such data, the horizontal and vertical movements, migratory behaviours and habitat use of Common Skate can be described. This is the first study to examine the finer-scale seasonal behaviours of Common Skate in the Celtic Sea and has implications with regards to assessing the vulnerability of these species to fishing activities.

title: The Great Eggcase Hunt: using citizen science to map species presence and diversity
abstract_text: The Great Eggcase Hunt has now been running for 13 years. In that time, over 130,000 eggcases have been recorded from 13 oviparous species found in UK waters along with additional species submitted from further afield (including the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the USA, Australia, Israel and South Africa). The project has been launched in the Netherlands and is currently being developed for Portugal and the US Eastern Seaboard. Spawning and nursery grounds are ecologically-important habitats, yet surprisingly little is known about the locations of such sites for skate and oviparous sharks in the Northeast Atlantic. While the Great Eggcase Hunt started out as a means to engage the public in shark conservation, the data generated is capable of much more and could lead to the identification of critical grounds used during the static life history phase of oviparous chondrichthyans, and could inform on potential options for spatial management. Measurements derived from specimens submitted to the Great Eggcase Hunt, those collected by CEFAS, museum collections and specimens from public aquaria underpinned a paper published earlier this year which provides updated descriptions and a revised taxonomic key to the eggcases of the British Isles. The next step is to overlay verified eggcase records with known captures of adults and juveniles. To enhance public interest, new identification guides have been created, a smartphone app (containing a step-by-step identification key, species profiles and a recording function) is available on iOS and Android devices and a newly released public report provides an update of the project to date.

title: Assessing the effectiveness of small MPAs for the recovery of an endangered elasmobranch - the Undulate Ray Raja undulata

authors.affiliation: CCMAR Centre of Marine Sciences of Algarve

abstract_text: Sharks and rays (Elasmobranchii) are nowadays reported as the most threatened marine fishes in Europe, and shelf water species are considered potentially more vulnerable. The Undulate Ray Raja undulata is coastal species classified as endangered, and it is currently target of specific fisheries regulation (on-board retention of this species is restricted since 2009 by the European Union). Although some studies have focused on biological aspects of this species such as growth, reproduction and feeding, little is known about its movement patterns and response to spatial protection. We studied the spatial dynamics of this species in a small marine protected area located in the north-eastern Atlantic, the Luiz Saldanha Marine Park (Portugal). Acoustic telemetry data was collected from May 2014 to June 2016 in the fully protected area and adjacent partially protected area. Data showed a high residence index of this species in the study area. Some individuals exhibited year-round residency in the reserve, while others were not solely restricted to the fully protected area and migrated to the adjacent partially protected areas. Movements were predominantly longitudinal along the coast and individuals generally remained at depths shallower than 40m, confirming this species preference for coastal habitats. Our results suggest that spatial closures are an appropriate measure for the conservation of undulate ray populations, and that even small reserves can offer some protection to this species. However, the recovery of healthy populations regarding abundance and genetics would be favoured by MPAs enclosing extended sections of coastal habitats.

title: Diver observations of individually recognisable Raja undulata provides detail of their site fidelity
abstract_text: The return of individual Undulate Rays to one known UK ray congregation site has been monitored over a three year period. This has included building and maintaining a database of all ray sightings. Ray identity is established from analysis of divers' photographs that include juvenile and fully mature rays. The data confirms and enhances the knowledge on the site fidelity of rays. Further analysis of congregation sites may provide important information on the behaviour and sustainability of rays.

title: Diel vertical migration in benthic predators
abstract_text: Diel vertical migration (DVM) is a well-documented behaviour where many pelagic marine species, from zooplankton to sharks, make vertical migrations through the water column, usually from deeper waters during the day to shallower waters at night. DVM in benthic predators is unexpected although recent studies observed DVM in catshark Scyliorhinus canicula and Burbot Lota lota. These DVMs, however, are an inshore–offshore movement across the bottom substrate. We present new observations of DVM in 4 species of skates; Raja brachyura, R. clavata, R. microocellata and R. montagui. During analysis of 89 archival tags, recording depth and temperature, 674 events were found in which the skate left a deeper phase, travelled greater than 5 m shallower, remained shallower for between 1 and 18 hours and returned to a depth within 2.5 m of the starting depth, suggesting possible site fidelity linked to central place foraging. Results suggest that partial DVM is highly variable but occurs in all 4 species with no significant differences in frequency. Further characteristics of the behaviour are presented as well as possible hypotheses for its occurrence. A greater understanding of where species occur in space and time are fundamental to conservation and management. Spatial distribution for instance, is crucial in assessing population trends of mobile animals. The daily movement of skates into and out of specific locations can influence measurements of population density and therefore our understanding of the population status of these vulnerable species.

title: Life history and reproductive biology of four mobulid species in the Bohol Sea, Philippines

abstract_text: A targeted fishery for mobulids (Mobula thurstoni, M. japanica, M. tarapacana and Manta birostris) operates seasonally in the Bohol Sea, Philippines. While M. birostris, has been protected in the Philippines since 1998, no protection or national fishery regulation exist for the other species. Description of life-history and reproductive parameters are fundamental to improving demographic models and support fishery management plans. Between November 2015-June 2016, over 2780 mobulids were caught by the fishery. We collected length and reproductive data from 1510 specimens landed, and we estimated from length-weight relationship that over 154 tons of M. thurstoni and M. japanica together were landed this season. Size-at-birth was reviewed for three species (e.g. 200-210cm for M. birostris), and represented up to 45% the mean maternal size. Sexual maturity was assessed by visual examination, to estimate size-at-maturity and size-at-pregnancy. Females matured at larger size (e.g. 163.6±0.6cm, DW±SE for M. thurstoni) than males (e.g. 158.4±0.9cm, DW±SE for M. thurstoni), and females did not systematically reproduce immediately after reaching maturity. For M. thurstoni, only 9% (n=64) of females which just reached maturity were pregnant. Size-at-pregnancy was estimated at 171.5±0.8cm (DW±SE) for this species. The development of the follicles is not always synchronous with the gestation, supporting evidence of a rest period between pregnancies. For M. thurstoni, up to 38% of mature females were pregnant during particular months suggesting peak reproduction, although fetus-size distributions did not show a clear seasonality in the reproductive cycles at the population level. Our results demonstrate the conservative life-history parameters of these species, and the necessity for local and international fishery regulation.

title: Environmental Enrichment on Captive Juvenile Thornback Rays, Raja clavata (Linnaeus 1758)
abstract_text: There are few studies investigating captive conditions for commonly kept public aquaria species. Here the Thornback Ray Raja clavata was used to determine preferred captive conditions via choice tests and behavioural observations. Substrate type, substrate colour, substrate depth, group size and refuge use were all used to assess usage, number of stereotypic behaviours and activity in captive born rays. Sand was the preferred choice of substrate which also brought fewer surface breaking behaviours (a possible stereotypic behaviour) compared to gravel or bare tanks. Lighter colours of sand were preferred, as were deeper depths whilst increasing group size increased possible stereotypic behaviours. Type of resting behaviour (horizontal vs vertical) also differed within experiments − rays switched from horizontal to vertical resting, on the side of the tank when using gravelled versus sandy areas of the tank. The rays in this study appeared not to use refuges. Very few published studies have focused on what aquatic animals want, here we use preference tests, which are a useful way of determining what the animal wants, and can help aquarists provide the best conditions for captive Thornback Rays.

title: Annotated List of the Batoids from off the Algerian Coast

authors.affiliation: Ecole Supérieure des Sciences de la Mer et de l'Aménagement du Littoral (ENSSMAL)
Ecole Supérieure des Sciences de la Mer et de l'Aménagement du Littoral (ENSSMAL)

abstract_text: Cartilaginous fish gathers sharks, batoids and chimaeras; in Mediterranean, according to the literature 51 sharks species and 17 skates species occur in the area. About 85 cartilaginous fish (considering the following genus: Squatina, Rhinobatos, Dasyatis, Taeniura, Gymnura, Mobular, Torpedo and Chimaera) are reported in total. Regular visits to fish markets of Algiers and marine surveys permit to up-date the list of Elasmobranchs (angelsharks, stingrays, devil rays, butterfly rays) and records were compared to former lists (Dieuzeide & al., 1953; Lalami, 1970). Twelve species of batoids (belonging to six families) have been recorded, using international identification keys (Bauchot and Pras, 1980; Compagno, 1984; Whitehead & al., 1986; Fisher et al., 1987) by examining and accurately identifying specimens. The sawfish completely disappeared from the Algerian basin and even from the whole Mediterranean although it was present in 1953. Angel sharks became very rare; two species occur. As regards to giant rays, there is a significant change: Mobular japanica occurs in the Mediterranean (Hemida & al,, 2016). M. japonica and M. mobular are closely related species leading to misidentifications. Batoids may be considered less frequent inhabitants of the Algerian basin at least, in the last few years. These species are present in the markets and are consumed like the other commercial fish.

title: A moving target: marine protected area conservation of reef sharks
abstract_text: The potential of marine protected areas (MPAs) to conserve sharks has been a topic of discussion and exploration for several years. Although it has been purported that closed areas will protect shark species, there is limited data to support this claim and inform spatial management actions. Here we discuss the results of four years of movement data from three species of shark in the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) Marine Park. Acoustic receivers were deployed at 17 reefs in the central GBR with reefs open and closed to fishing represented. Residency of sharks at individual reefs varied by species. The most resident species, the Grey Reef Shark, was detected 80% of the time, while the more pelagic Silvertip Shark was only detected 50% of the time and larger species such as Bull Sharks were detected as little as 20% of the time. The number of reefs visited also varied by species and in some cases by sex indicating varying levels of benefit from MPA zones. These data have been useful in assisting the GBR Marine Park Authority to define the efficacy of the multi-use spatial planning design and indicate that reef level protection may not be adequate to protect mobile species. Differences in movement patterns among species mean a single approach may not be adequate and that conservation and management may need to be species specific. Understanding spatial ecology of predators is key to effective reef-based conservation planning.

title: The Global Shark Tracking Project: worldwide analysis of movements, space-use, hotspots and fisheries interactions

authors.affiliation: Marine Biological Association of the UK
Marine Biological Association of the UK
Marine Biological Association of the UK

authors.full_name: the Global Shark Tracking Project Consortium

abstract_text: Overfishing is arguably the greatest ecological threat facing the oceans, yet catches of many highly migratory fishes including pelagic sharks remain largely unregulated with poor monitoring and data reporting. Shark conservation is hampered by basic knowledge gaps about where sharks aggregate across population ranges and precisely where they overlap with fishers. The Global Shark Tracking Project was initiated to address these issues by assembling unique global datasets of satellite tracks of pelagic sharks and commercial fishing vessels. The objectives of the consortium of over 40 research groups worldwide are to: (1) map shark and vessel distributions globally, (2) relate them to the changing ocean environment, and (3) identify any hotspots and estimate overlaps. The study will explore the future role of combining fine-scale fish and vessel telemetry to inform the ocean-scale management of shark fisheries. In this presentation I will describe the research leading to the project's foundation and will provide details about its progress.

title: The Amsterdam Effect: multiple stakeholder cooperation for successful management of sharks and rays
abstract_text: The management of sharks and rays in European fisheries is both complex and challenging. Compounding factors are paucity of data, the group TAC for skates and rays and the uncertainties surrounding the landing obligation, whereby the species could choke the target fisheries. Cooperation between multiple stakeholders is essential to address these issues. In order to do this, the Dutch Elasmobranch Society has organized a number of expert meetings in Amsterdam. The meetings were attended by scientists, administrators and representatives from the fishing industry and NGOs from six European countries. Possible solutions and ways forward were discussed and the delegates gave their support for the continuation of the platform and working towards solutions. In the coming years the partners in this project will work on developing a two track approach to addressing key issues and questions. On the one hand we will work on a science-industry partnership on solutions to collect essential information on bycatch and survival of elasmobranchs. On the other hand we will set up a dialogue platform with all stakeholders, in which ideas can be developed, coalitions formed and concrete solutions found. The resulting proposals to policy makers will have a high chance of successful implementation because they are supported by all relevant stakeholders. This unique approach combines multiple levels of influence. This presentation will present the first results of the multi-stakeholder process and co-production of knowledge for the management of elasmobranchs.

title: Management implications of partial migration by Tiger Sharks in the Northwest Atlantic
abstract_text: Without understanding what factors inform shark movement decisions, assessments of interactions with area-focused human activities, such as fishing, and efforts to mitigate these interactions may be severely hindered. In the northwest Atlantic, Tiger Sharks are regularly caught in high seas fisheries, and have been shown to undertake long distance, partial migrations between coral reef and open ocean habitats. We used generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) to reveal how variation in intrinsic (e.g. size) and extrinsic factors (e.g. habitat suitability, prey availability) influenced migratory behaviour, and assessed how these migrations influence fisheries interactions and potential management strategies. We revealed that large Tiger Sharks primarily associated with a narrow thermal niche and areas of high primary productivity, while smaller sharks experienced a much broader range of temperatures and much weaker associations with productivity, indicating an ontogenetic shift in drivers of movements and migrations. The observed migration patterns have significant management implications: existing shark sanctuaries (Bahamas, British Virgin Islands, Saba) only covered 12% of Tiger Shark movements, although this could be increased to 52% through designation of Bermuda's exclusive economic zone as a shark sanctuary. However, evaluation of potential fisheries interactions revealed that over 80% of potential interactions would still occur outside of shark sanctuaries, requiring combination with other management interventions such as gear modification or quotas.

title: Predicting natural mortality in elasmobranchs
abstract_text: Natural mortality is a crucial parameter to assess the status of species. However, it is inherently difficult to observe directly in nature and most commonly indirect methods are utilized to estimate natural mortality based on other life history parameters. These relationships are almost exclusively based on bony fish data and their performance for elasmobranchs is unclear due to a lack of data for this group. Here, we will present 15 direct estimates of natural mortality from 10 different elasmobranch species obtained from newly analysed datasets and an extensive literature review which is to our knowledge the world's most comprehensive dataset of its kind. We will discuss the performance of the most commonly applied indirect methods and give recommendations on best practices to estimate the natural mortality rate in elasmobranchs and other animals.

title: Sharks at risk? Ecological risk assessment and shark productivity in the Dutch Caribbean
abstract_text: The Dutch Caribbean islands are home to over 24 elasmobranch species, half of which are considered threatened with extinction according to IUCN guidelines. Over the past decades, local populations appear to have declined drastically, most probably due to fishing and loss of suitable habitat. There is a persistent lack of (baseline) data on their occurrence, spatial distribution, and population structure, which is an incentive for extensive biological research to scope the problem and underpin management advice. The utility of Ecological Risk Assessments is considered an effective tool to theoretically assess the vulnerability to fishing and habitat degradation of species for which there is little information available. For elasmobranch species, a semi-quantitative approach such as Productivity Susceptibility Analysis (PSA) may provide some insight into conservation and management priorities by assessing threats to the population status of individual species. We did a first exploration into the impact of fishing on Dutch Caribbean shark species following the hierarchical Ecological Risk Assessment for the Effects of Fishing (ERAEF) approach. We show the preliminary results of 14 species that were assessed using a PSA analysis and identify further data needs to effectively base future conservation action and management decisions.

title: Characterising a potential multi-species shark nursery area in a tropical estuary in Fiji
abstract_text: Studies focusing on environmental factors that influence the distribution of juvenile sharks in shark nurseries and essential habitats are still scarce in the literature. Anthropogenic stresses such as overfishing and habitat destruction urge for improved holistic conservation and fishery management approaches to respond to decreasing shark abundances in many areas. Investigating species-specific environmental preferences and identifying potential nursery areas provides much needed scientific baseline data that can support long-term decisions and aid the protection of threatened species in respective regions. In Fiji, knowledge on sharks is still limited, though scientific investigations are increasing. This study assessed juvenile shark abundances in a tropical estuary in north-western Viti Levu, Fiji, by conducting a fishery-independent survey over the course of five months. Additionally, potential abiotic drivers of juvenile shark distribution were investigated and average shark catch composition on the local fish market was monitored over a period of 67 days. Three shark species were observed within the estuary; Carcharhinus limbatus, Sphyrna lewini and Sphyrna mokarran. Depth, turbidity and proximity to mangroves were identified as the most influential drivers, although relative importance differed among shark species. The condition of umbilical scars (70 % open or semi-healed) and observed mean sizes of captured individuals strongly suggest that the Ba estuary area serves as a parturition ground for at least two of the present species (S. lewini, C. limbatus) and may consequently be utilized as a nursery ground. Thus, this study offers valuable insights into the early life-stages of three shark species in the Central Pacific.

title: Uncovering the migratory behaviours of deep-water sharks and the implications for fisheries management
abstract_text: Our poor understanding of deep-water shark life history and their ecological role within continental slope environments is of concern in light of current heavy fishing pressures. The life-long movements of individual sharks govern population connectivity, potential roles in ecosystem structuring and vulnerability to fishing pressure. Unravelling individual movement behaviour is challenging in most oceanic elasmobranchs, but especially so for deep-water fishes where smart tags and mark-recapture studies are seldom practical. Here we use bulk carbon and nitrogen stable isotope analysis, of both sharks and the wider fish community, and a long-term catch-abundance survey to uncover both spatial and trophic dynamics within a bathyal shark assemblage at Rockall Trough. Furthermore, we present stable isotope data from incrementally-grown tissues from two historically exploited deep-water sharks species, the Leafscale Gulper Shark Centrophorus squamosus and the Portuguese Dogfish Centroscymnus coelolepis from the Northeast Atlantic. We report the first direct evidence for ontogenetic shifts in depth and large-scale latitudinal migrations for individual deep-water sharks within the northeast Atlantic. Isotopic evidence for individual movements compliments genetic data quantifying population-scale connectivity. Comparisons of life history movements of these species with other deep-water fishes from Northeast Atlantic allow us to explore the ecological role that these sharks play and the potential consequences of their declines. Although zero total allowable catches (TACs) are enforce within Europe, evidence provided here suggests this may only offer partial protection during the ontogenetic movements of larger, highly migratory shark species.

title: Sexual maturity of the Velvet Belly Shark Etmopterus spinax in the north east Atlantic
abstract_text: The Velvet Belly Shark is a small deep-sea shark living in the eastern Atlantic and in the Mediterranean Sea. Despite the prohibition for deep-sea shark species, they are very sensitive to overexploitation and are facing un-reported by-catches. Moreover, deep-sea sharks have an important role in maintaining a balance in their respective food webs, and are particularly vulnerable to commercial fishing pressures due to their slow growth rates and low reproductive capacity. This is worsened by the fact that basic biological information in order to support sustainable management of fisheries at appropriate spatial scales, is lacking for this species. This paper is the result of the sampling analysis in 3 different areas of the Atlantic (n=798): the southern region of the Bay of Biscay, the Celtic Sea and the off the northeast of Scotland from 2013 to 2015 and at depths between 400 and 500 meters. This study measured the maturity stage range between local distributions to assess ecological parameters in a deep-sea shark, Etmopterus spinax, and discusses impacts on their conservation.

title: Ontogenetic changes in the Velvet Belly Lanternshark Etmopterus spinax in the Balearic Sea: implications on the taxonomy of the genus

authors.affiliation: Marine Biology Laboratory, Departament of Zoology, Universitat de València
Marine Biology Laboratory, Departament of Zoology, Universitat de València; IROX: Institut de Recerca Oceanogràfica de Xàbia
Marine Biology Laboratory, Departament of Zoology, Universitat de València

abstract_text: Classic shark taxonomy has been historically based on biometric relationships between body measurements. Nevertheless, variations during ontogeny or due to sexual dimorphism often have not been taken into account. This situation makes difficult the correct identification and new descriptions of species of the genus, which is essential for conservation and fisheries management issues. Morphometric trends of 73 body measurements in the mesopelagic shark Etmopterus spinax from 116 specimens caught in the Gulf of Valencia (Western Mediterranean) have been studied. Existence of sexual dimorphism has been detected in only 9.5% of such measurements, but 97.3% showed allometric trends at least in one of the sexes. A remarkable allometric trend revealing the existence of appreciable differences of shape between new-borns and adults has been detected in 27% of measurements. Among these, it is remarkable a clear negative allometric trend in cephalic and caudal regions, a positive allometry in visceral region and different trends, but close to isometry, of most measurements related with paired fins. Ontogenetic variation of several taxonomic characters used in taxonomy of the genus Etmopterus has been analysed. Such characters, defined as ratios between body measurements, have shown a high variability due to morphometric changes during ontogeny. The presented results intend to provide a pattern of ontogenetic changes that could be extrapolated to related species, to stablish useful taxonomic characters for the genus. In this sense, we suggest the use of body measurements characters showing in E. spinax isometric patterns, or with ratios among measurements showing similar allometric coefficients.

title: Study of swimming capabilities of Etmopterus spinax, the Velvet Belly Lanternshark, inferred by muscle enzyme activities

abstract_text: Although, 50 shark species are described as luminous, their ecology is still poorly known while they represent about 10 percent of all shark species. One small deep-sea model shark species, Etmopterus spinax (Linnaeus 1758), living in eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, has attracted a lot of attention. Studies have shown that E. spinax use the luminescence to avoid predators by a camouflage called counterillumination (when emitted light is similar than downwelling sunlight at depth, to cloak the silhouette from below). Other studies have shown that the regulation of its light intensity is hormonal and therefore is very slow. This leads to the conclusion that E.spinax, although able to counterilluminate, needed to vertically migrate in the water column in order to stay in a constant ambient light level to keep the efficiency of this camouflage. This hypothesis was called the isolume-follower. Recent work, bring some support to this hypothesis. Indeed, the swimming speed of height deep-water shark species were evaluated from footages analysis and showed that Etmopteridae luminescent sharks have a higher cruise swimming speed than non-luminescent counterparts. Here, we investigated E. spinax muscle activities through three different enzymes which can infer about the swimming capabilities of this species. Results show higher aerobic enzyme activities for E. spinax than for a non-luminescent counterpart, Centroscylium fabricii in red and white muscles. About the anaerobic enzyme activities, no significant difference is observed between both species. These results support the use of high cruise speed of luminescent sharks to fulfill the isolume-follower hypothesis.

title: Distribution and ecology of Hexanchus griseus in the Cantabrian Sea (NE Atlantic)

title: Notorynchus cepedianus in Aotearoa, New Zealand

title: Trophic cascades and Cownose Ray scapegoats: Save the Bay - Eat a Ray and the effects of confirmation bias on elasmobranch conservation

authors.affiliation: Florida State University Coastal and Marine Laboratory

abstract_text: Top-down versus bottom-up control of marine ecosystems has been debated for decades. Large sharks are frequently described as "apex predators" that maintain ecosystem health by controlling prey populations, but evidence to support shark-mediated top-down effects is limited. Declines in shark populations led to a surge in research seeking cascading effects of predator removals on lower trophic levels. In the northwest Atlantic Ocean, a highly cited paper in Science Magazine claimed depletion of large sharks caused dramatic increases in Cownose Ray populations which led to collapses of commercial bivalve stocks due to ray predation. These claims were used to justify a Cownose Ray fishery under the slogan 'Save the Bay, Eat a Ray'. Human consumption of the rays and killing them for sport were touted as environmentally responsible mechanisms to promote recovery of estuaries and shellfish stocks. We evaluated the evidence for this trophic cascade and found the conclusions were unsupported at all trophic levels. We demonstrated that Cownose Rays have among the most vulnerable elasmobranch life histories suggesting that current harvest rates may be unsustainable. This study highlights the danger of confirmation bias in conservation biology. Sensational scientific claims garner media attention and high citation rates by scientists, even if the studies are challenged in the literature as being severely flawed. Objectivity, scepticism and acknowledgment of uncertainty are critical components to scientific research and robust peer-review. Confirmation bias not only damages scientific credibility, but may also promote misguided conservation measures that may have negative unintended consequences.

title: Catching angels: Habitat use, population structure and growth rates of juvenile Angelsharks Squatina squatina in a nursery area

abstract_text: The Angelshark Squatina squatina is one of the most endangered fish species in Europe, listed as Critically Endangered. Once common throughout the Atlantic and Europe's seas, they are now extinct from much of their former range, leaving the Canary Islands as the last remaining stronghold. Whereas the presence of Angelsharks around the Canary Islands is known, information about nursery grounds and the ecology of neonates and juveniles is majorly lacking. This study investigated a unique nursery ground at Tenerife Island, using a tag-recapture study since 2015, to (1) describe habitat use and population structure, to (2) work out growth rates and (3) relativeness among juvenile Angelsharks. Surveys were only conducted at night, in sandy lower shore areas between 0.4-5 m depth. Preliminary results show that juvenile Angelsharks exhibit a long-term residency of at least 5 – 6 months. title: Environmental DNA detects Critically Endangered Largetooth Sawfish in the wild
abstract_text: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is a relatively new tool for the detection of rare, threatened and invasive species in water bodies. In this study we investigated the utility of an eDNA approach in detecting the Critically Endangered Largetooth Sawfish Pristis pristis in freshwater habitats in northern Australia. Water samples were collected from a large aquaria mesocosm containing sawfish and other aquatic species, and floodplain waterholes and the main river channel of the Daly River, Northern Territory. Water samples were filtered using a 20 µm nylon filter. DNA was extracted from filters and analysed with PCR using species-specific mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (COI) primers designed to amplify only Largetooth Sawfish DNA. PCR products were cleaned and the COI gene sequenced to confirm the species identity. Testing using this method using three aquaria, one containing a Largetooth Sawfish, positively identified sawfish only in the correct aquarium. In the field water samples, seven of eight floodplain waterholes produced a sawfish eDNA PCR product, while eDNA was not detected in the main river channel. Based on gillnet sampling and traditional ecological knowledge, sawfish were known to occur at half of the waterhole and floodplain sites that tested positive for sawfish eDNA. These results demonstrated that an eDNA approach to detecting Largeooth Sawfish can produce reliable results and can be used as a survey tool to help with conservation efforts for this and other threatened elasmobranchs.

title: Can all roads lead to sawfish? Experimental eDNA sampling for sawfish in coastal seawaters, a preliminary work in western Africa
abstract_text: Sawfishes (Pristidae) are facing on of the most critical conservation issue worldwide despite the increase of their protection and research. In Western Africa, the two species (Pristis pristis and P. pectinata) are still present in localised areas that deserve more investigation. Biological and ecological knowledge of rare species is a thorny challenge that may be solve by indirect methods such as tagging or genetic. A recent development of environmental DNA (eDNA) offers a smart way to post-track animal presence. By combining data from current distribution of sawfish and an experimental sampling designed for remote areas, we've been testing 4 samples from substrate and water column collected in coastal seawaters of Guinea Bissau (AMP Urok, Bijagos Islands). These results are compared and discussed with aquarium sampling in order to validate and improve this new promising field method that might be a perfect tool for conservation of sawfishes.

title: Endangered Species are Ten a Penny
abstract_text: Despite their extremely fragile state in the wild, sawfish specimens are ten a penny in museum collections. Sadly, the impressive nature of sawfish rostra historically led to them being collected in large numbers and transported around the world as curiosities. Could these vast collections be used as a resource for conservation biology, or are they just lifeless ambassadors for the species they represent? A number of studies have utilised museum specimens for scientific research. Specimens that have associated locality data have been used to identify and evaluate historical ranges. Given the extent to which populations have shrunk, many specimens record the presence of sawfish in areas where they are now locally extinct. Other studies have used rostral tooth counts of sawfish specimens held in museum collections to examine sexual dimorphism, bilateral asymmetry and to elucidate morphological characters for phylogenetic studies. These example studies demonstrate that these specimens have a valid use in scientific research in a bid to protect the species in the modern day. This talk outlines the many ways in which museum collections can aid conservation biology, and how museums can make their collections available for study.

title: Sawfishes: How to fight Rostrums Illegal Trade. Tools used against this French Internet Black Market supported by MEsR-Scie Project
abstract_text: Sawfish family (Pristidae) is recognized as one of the most in peril elasmobranch in the world. All species of sawfishes are listed as "Critically Endangered" on the Red List from the IUCN and some populations considered as locally extinct. Due to their long rostrum, sawfishes are particularly vulnerable to fisheries and the high value of their appendice is an incentive to the black market development. Sawfishes have been subject to exploitation since the 30's in different part of the world and their populations have drastically decreased. Their most important actual threat is by-catches and their post-uses. Since, 2012, DRDH has identified more than 300 rostrums in sell on French websites. Even if this trade is considered as illegal in the Washington Convention (Annex 1), the black market remains important and it could be an incentive on sawfishes over exploitation and may accelerate their extinction. To evaluate this incentive and to find solutions, DRDH has launched MEsR-SCIE Project in 2012. The on-going program will be discussed and tools used in order to prevent this illegal market and to sensitize sellers will be detailed: Websites monitoring, Public and Professional awareness, collaboration and exchanges with French Customs and moreover, legal action against professional taken by DRDH and France Nature Environnement (FNE).

abstract_text: ANGELSHARK-ID is a project created for long-term monitoring of Angelsharks Squatina squatina in the Canary Islands, employing photo-identification as a tool to generate scientific base knowledge contributing to the development of effective species management, while minimizing research impacts to the studied populations. abstract_text: The protection of the Angelshark Squatina squatina in its last remaining stronghold is of upmost importance. This unique species has been eliminated throughout much of its historical range over the past century and is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (Ferretti et al. 2015). The highest priority threats to Angelshark populations were identified and key steps to address these threats were discussed to build a comprehensive Action Plan. Our joint Vision for the Action Plan is that Angelsharks in the Canary Islands are abundant and protected in their unique stronghold. The Action Plan will be launched in Autumn 2016 and focuses around six main goals: Fisheries, Habitat & Pollution, Human Interaction, Legislation, Research and Community Engagement. title: Developing the best method to minimise the impact of recreational fishing in the Canary Islands for the Critically Endangered Angelshark

authors.affiliation: EcoAqua, Universidad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria (AngelShark Project)
Zoological Society of London (Angel Shark Project)

abstract_text: When working with a Critically Endangered species, in this case the Angelshark Squatina squatina, it is vital to have the cooperation of all actors involved, especially the recreational fishing community. The Angel Shark Project, have always wanted to forge a bond with everyone connected with the sea, especially the fishing and diving industries. The recreational fishing industry in the Canary Islands is extensive, with more than 130,000 licenses. In 2010, 47% of the total fishing catch was by recreational fishers. Recreational fishing in the Canary Islands can be classified into two areas: recreational fishermen and recreational fishing charter vessels where paying clients charter a boat to fish. However, there is a significant lack of data on recreational fishing activity, number of fishermen, method or species targeted. We know that at different times of year, recreational fishers use a deep or bottom method and during this period the number of Angelsharks caught greatly increase. In 2015, the Angel Shark Project developed a best practice guide to catch and release to minimize the impact and increase the survival of the Angelshark after accidental catch by recreational fishers in the Canary Island waters. In only two years we have involved more than 60% of all recreational fishing charter vessels in the Archipelago with more than 90% stake in each of the three visited islands. The success of this project lies with the continuous feedback between the Angel Shark Project, recreational fishermen and their clients with the use of community visits, questionnaires and e-messages.

title: Guitarfishes: can learning from the sawfish disaster prevent a similar fate?
abstract_text: Sawfishes and guitarfishes share numerous characteristics: they are large, economically valuable shark-like rays found in shallow warm water close to humans that are vulnerable to capture. Scientists and managers largely failed to recognise, document, and prevent catastrophic global declines of sawfishes, making most attempts at their recovery impossible or extraordinarily difficult. However, this experience can provide valuable lessons to try and ensure the same mistakes are not made for guitarfishes: a group that remains poorly researched, with alarming declines reported for some species. Guitarfish may be even more vulnerable to extinction than sawfishes, because some species have a very restricted distribution in only the poorest developing countries. This talk outlines what elasmobranch conservation can learn both from successes and failures in the conservation of other marine vertebrates, and from the much more mature field of terrestrial conservation.

title: Local indicators for global species: the case study of the Cabo Verde pelagic sharks captured within the EU Sustainable Fisheries Partnership Agreements

authors.affiliation: IPMA - Instituto Português do Mar e da Atmosfera (Portugal)

abstract_text: Pelagic sharks are an important bycatch in pelagic swordfish longline fisheries. In the Cabo Verde Archipelago (tropical NE Atlantic), pelagic shark catches can reach important levels, sometimes higher than the target species. Due to the increased concern on the status of shark species, an EU funded project (MARE/2012/21 - SC7) was developed to provide scientific advice on the conservation of pelagic sharks associated with the EU fishing activity, in a collaboration between several EU and Cabo Verde research Institutes. A satellite tagging program was established with the deployment of 30 satellite tags in Blue and Shortfin Mako Sharks in the Cabo Verde EEZ, showing that those species are highly mobile. Stock status indicators for the main species were created, including analysis of size frequency distributions over time and standardized catch-per-unit-of-effort (CPUE) indexes. The standardized CPUEs have been stable for the past 10 years, indicating no signs of local depletion. In terms of sizes, the Blue Shark catch is composed mainly of adults, which is a sign of a healthier population. By the contrary, the catch of Shortfin Mako is composed mainly of juveniles, which is a cause of concern. The biomass and size distributions were modelled with spatial and seasonal models (GAMs) identifying locations where juveniles are predominantly concentrated and that should be prioritized for conservation. This work presents new information on the status of pelagic sharks in the Cabo Verde region, and can now be used to promote more sustainable fisheries in the region.

title: A multi-disciplinary study of Tope Galeorhinus galeus in the North East Atlantic: site fidelity, seasonal movements and connectivity
abstract_text: Tope Galeorhinus galeus is a common elasmobranch throughout the NE Atlantic where landings have declined significantly with severe reductions especially notable in the Mediterranean. Previous studies have struggled to find consistent movement patterns in the region and the population is currently managed as a single stock throughout the NE Atlantic. A multidisciplinary approach consisting of tagging, both mark and recapture and archival, and genetic markers was undertaken to gain insight into Tope's regional movements and behaviour. Most Tope remained <500 km from their tagging site with some mature females displaying a wider, more southerly range including connectivity with the Mediterranean. Evidence of annual site fidelity was found in all age and sex classes. Data showed a mature male and female moving off the continental shelf to depths >800 m with some evidence of a sex dependent north/south preference. An 858-bp fragment of the mitochondrial control region (mtDNA) and eight focal microsatellite markers (µSAT) were used to explore gene flow throughout the NE Atlantic and the MED. Overall, genetic diversity was found to be relatively low with haplotype and nucleotide diversities of 0.59 and 0.001 respectively and a mean allelic richness of 4.34 in the nuclear DNA. Genetic differentiation was homogenous across sampling sites for both markers with no significant differentiation detected indicating gene flow through the NE Atlantic and Mediterranean. This work provides new insight into the movements of Tope and should be constructive to future management of the species.

title: Identifying the last refuges for sharks

authors.affiliation: Institute of Zoology, Zoological Society of London

abstract_text: Identifying conservation priorities to counteract biodiversity loss has received considerable attention in terrestrial and – to lesser degree - in coral reef ecosystems. However, marine prioritisation in general remains challenged by a lack of information beyond classic geographic range maps and fishery data. Range maps and fishery data may not adequately reveal critical habitats required to sustain populations of threatened predators, which are unevenly distributed across shallow reefs, continental shelves, seamounts, and abyssal plains. Here we overcome this constraint with an extensive and novel survey to model top predator hotspots across territorial waters in the tropical Indo-Pacific using three metrics: vertebrate species richness, mean maximum body size, and shark abundance, thereby identifying critical habitats for designation of marine protected areas (MPAs). The last refuges for sharks were present at 1,200 km from markets, whereas the last refuges for body size were found at 950 km, suggesting that marine ecosystems have limited capacity to buffer shark depletions. Proximity to populations and markets combined explained 21 and 12.5 % of the variance in body size and shark abundance respectively, reflecting a human footprint that is likely to increase with developments in fishing gear and fuel efficiency. Our analyses reveals that the last predator hotspots will be supported on shallow seabed features such as seamounts, submerged banks, and continental slopes that are remote from human populations and markets. We show that these hotspots locations are currently underrepresented within MPAs deemed effective at protecting predators, and should therefore be prioritised for effective MPA designation.

title: The Cayman Islands Shark & Ray Sanctuary: research and public awareness inputs

abstract_text: In April 2015 the Cayman Islands Government enacted legislation giving full protection to all elasmobranchs throughout Cayman waters. This achievement was the result of an eight year research and public awareness programme. The occurrence and abundance of sharks and rays was investigated using a) a public (diver) reporting scheme, b) extensive surveys with baited remote underwater video stations (BRUVS), and c) scientific long-lining and tagging. The data revealed moderately good populations of Caribbean Reef, Nurse and Black-tip Sharks, and smaller numbers of other species including Great Hammerhead and Tiger Sharks. Some sharks were fitted with acoustic tags, showing that Caribbean Reef Sharks may move between separate islands (up to 100 km), while the Tiger Sharks visit Cayman seasonally during migration throughout the Caribbean. Socio-economic studies demonstrated that not only is the well-known Stingray City / Sand Cay site the highest grossing tourist attraction in the Caribbean, but the possibility of seeing sharks and other marine megafauna is worth a further $100 million per year to the Caymans' economy. Public awareness projects have included talks to schools, publicity through the local brewery and a supermarket chain, outreach to fishers (including individual interviews and the formation of fisher support groups), public awareness events directed at government and other key stakeholders, and a public awareness campaign using newspapers, radio and TV. While a small minority of fishers still resent the new legislation, the overwhelming majority of both residents and visitors are highly supportive of the shark and ray protection measures.

title: White Shark's presence and behaviour related to the ecotourism at Guadalupe Island, México
abstract_text: The White Shark ecotourism at Guadalupe Island is the main activity for the exploitation of this resource in Mexico. However, the use of baits has caused some concern because its effect on White Sharks at the island is unknown. Our study aims to determine the effect of different types of bait on the presence and behaviour of white sharks. The type of bait, sightings, behaviour and pictures for Photo ID were recorded aboard tourist boats that used both legal and illegal baits during August-November 2012-2014. The data were analysed according to sex, maturity and the total of sharks, in relation to the type of bait. The recording of behaviour will determine the degree of individual conditioning of white sharks, based on interaction times and consumption of baits. We recorded 6,480 sightings during 98 days, which 26% were female and 71% male (1:3 H:M; U= 1521.5; p < 0.05); 48% were identified as juveniles and 49%, as adults; for both the 3% were indeterminate organisms. Regarding to the presence according to the type of bait (n = 4), no category showed a significantly higher frequency of sightings. To describe the behaviour is necessary to conclude with the identification of individuals, but so far, has been revised 80% of the audio-visual record (n = 17,360 files). With this we have already identified 79 sharks, 21 which are new records for the population TB in Guadalupe Island.

title: Biotelemetry reveals complex interactions between White Sharks and ecosystem engineers
abstract_text: White Sharks Carcharodon carcharias are known to aggregate in areas associated with prey, such as waters around seal colonies. White Sharks at such a site, near Gansbaai, South Africa, were initially tagged with ultrasonic, active acoustic tags and manually tracked into and around areas dense in kelp and reef. Further predation studies revealed Cape Fur Seals utilise the same areas as a refuge, although the nature of sub-surface interactions between White Sharks, their prey, and ecosystem engineers remained unknown. Recent advances in biotelemetry have the potential to reveal complex behaviours within these sites. We are now deploying biologging tags with cameras, triaxial accelerometers, magnetometers, gyroscopes and depth, temperature, light and speed sensors to White Sharks in these regions. Data from these tags are providing new insights into foraging behaviours and interactions between White Sharks and their prey.

title: Automated White Shark photo identification: towards an international fin-printing database
abstract_text: We present a fully automated photo identification system for recognising the fins of individual White Sharks. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first fully automated contour-based animal biometrics system. In order to recognise individuals, we combine robust fin contour detection with a multi-scale and combinatorial representation of fin shape. This enables individual sharks to be recognised efficiently and accurately, even when images are unclear or the view of the fin is partly blocked. Overall, the photo identification system demonstrates promising performance in recognising individuals with no need for manual labelling and with an average compute time of one minute per image. On a test-bed dataset representing 85 individuals, up to 82 per cent of images are correctly classified, with a further 10 per cent of correct matches occurring within the top 10 identities returned. The objective for the current phase of the project is to integrate photo identification and online data management technologies to build a scalable and easy-to-use, multi-user white shark fin-printing database. We report the progress that has been made on this transition from our test-bed system and outline the challenges that lie ahead.

title: The potential for using remote camera-traps to detect changes in the population trends of pelagic sharks
abstract_text: Effective monitoring of pelagic shark populations in the absence of fisheries data, such as in marine reserves, is a significant challenge. Remote camera-traps have the potential to monitor pelagic sharks, but remain largely untested. Within a simulated environment, we developed a method that modified existing gas models to investigate the number of camera-traps needed to detect pelagic shark populations trends over a five-year period in both un-baited and baited (divided into full- and partial-detection) arrays. We assessed the accuracy and precision of trend estimates obtained from camera trap arrays under different scenarios of population sizes of different spatial and temporal distributions undergoing varying levels of population change. Our results demonstrated that across un-baited and both baited models, scenarios with larger starting populations, faster rates of change, heterogeneous distributions, and absence of seasonal variation required smaller camera-trap arrays to produce accurate and precise population trend estimates. We concluded that camera-trap arrays could serve as a useful fisheries-independent method to monitor pelagic sharks. However, unless the population size is large and/or changing at a high rate, significant numbers of baited camera-traps would be required. Unfortunately, such large arrays would come with significant financial and labour costs and therefore may not be a realistic monitoring option.

abstract_text: In the Mid-Atlantic Azores, the emergence of a seasonal ecotourism shark diving industry strongly contrasts with a North Atlantic shark fishery for regional, national and foreign fleets. Shark diving may provide an economic alternative to fishing, promoting an ecological and economical sustainable use of these animals, favouring their conservation. Understanding socio-economic aspects of this new Mid-Atlantic industry is the first step towards its sustainability and ultimately shark conservation. Data were collected by means of questionnaire designed to solicit information on shark divers' knowledge, socio-economic status, expenditures and expectations, conducted between July and August 2014 on Pico and Faial Islands, to 144 divers. Finally, it is worth saying that nearly 70% of participants were willing to pay an extra amount until 60€ to ensure that shark diving remains an option and more than half (53%) would like to see that amount invested in conservation.

title: Records of rare chondrichthyan fishes in the North to the Baltic Sea
abstract_text: Records of rare chondrichthyan fishes to the North Sea, the transitional waters and the Baltic Sea have been collated from literature, museum collections, scientific surveys and landings data. Lusitanian species, that have their main distribution areas in more southerly and warmer waters, have likely taken migration routes during the summer through the English Channel or around the British Isles to enter the North Sea and migrated further on. Among these are specimens of Alopias vulpinus, Carcharhinus longimanus, Cetorhinus maximus, Dasyatis pastinaca, Myliobatis aquila, Prionace glauca, Pristis pectinata, P. pristis, Squatina squatina, Torpedo marmorata, and T. nobiliana, which have been recorded in the past. Boreal and deep-water species from the northern North and the Norwegian Sea, such as Chimaera monstrosa, Hexanchus griseus, Leucoraja fullonica, Rajella lintea, and Somniosus microcephalus, have done migrations probably in the winter into the area and are also presented with exceptional southerly occurrences in the southern North Sea, the Skagerrak, and Kattegat. Often, records are historic ones, showing that widely migrating specimens were able to reach the area in former times. Fisheries landings data show a rise of landings of some species in adjacent waters, such as in the Bay of Biscay or the English Channel, with a simultaneous disappearance of records of these summer guests in the considered area, indicating that fishing pressure could be responsible for their today's absence.

title: Trialling smartphones for improved fisheries data collection and monitoring - lessons learned from Madagascar
abstract_text: Fisheries and aquaculture support the livelihoods of at least 10 percent of the world's population, yet 75 percent of fish stocks are either fully or overexploited, with severe declines reported for many elasmobranch species. Reversing this trend requires improved management, which depends on accurate stock status data. Yet, the majority of fisheries, in particular small-scale fisheries in the developing world, are unmonitored. Recent advances in technology and the rapid extension of mobile networks in Africa have seen new data collection systems being utilised. This study reports lessons learned from the first trial (2013-2015) using smartphones as data collection tools, in the data deficient, traditional elasmobranch fishery of SW Madagascar. A network of 13 community data collectors, along 40 km of remote coastline, were trained to record shark landings using smartphones. At the end of the trial period, data were being successfully collected by community members and sent directly to an online database, where they can be accessed instantly, facilitating quick analysis and data-sharing, providing the community, and other stakeholders with an almost real-time view of local resource use. The main challenges encountered were the lack of infrastructure, poor levels of education and limited prior knowledge of technology within the community. The project worked closely with community members to develop suitable mobile data collection and training tools. The project demonstrates that mobile technology can empower fishers and other stakeholders to collect important data to support adaptive fisheries management, and the potential for this approach to be adapted to broader-scale multi-species fisheries.

title: Does personality reflect space use in wild juvenile Lemon Sharks?
abstract_text: Animal personality is defined as consistent individual behaviour over time and across situations, and inter-individual differences suggest different personality types. Surprisingly, in large marine vertebrates the widespread application of acoustic telemetry has rarely explored this framework to explain intraspecific variations in movement. Here, we tested if personality scores, derived from open-field tests, can be used as a proxy to predict space use in wild juvenile Lemon Sharks Negaprion brevirostris. Across two years, 29 individuals (pre-caudal length = 52.5 ± 1.7 cm) were captured in Bimini, Bahamas, and repeatedly tested in a novel open-field. Upon release they were subsequently tracked for 9 months with internal acoustic transmitters using active and passive methods. Results reveal a significant relationship between wild home-range size (kernel utilization distribution 50% and 95%) and personality in an open-field (Repeatability=0.51). Additionally, mean observed distance from shore was correlated to the personality score obtained in captivity. These results emphasize the importance of multidisciplinary approaches to movement ecology and behaviour research in large marine predators.

title: Of teeth and trees: fossil tip-dating the phylogeny of squaliform sharks

authors.affiliation: Bavarian State Collection of Zoology, Department Ichthyology, Munich, Germany

abstract_text: Dogfish sharks, or Squaliformes, are a monophyletic group of sharks, which predominantly occur in the deep sea. Most former studies, either based on morphological or molecular data, support the monophyly of Squaliformes, but also result in conflicting outcomes concerning squaliform interrelationships and origination age due to different node age estimations. Herein, we use fossil tip-dating, or total-evidence to simultaneously infer phylogenetic relationships and divergence times of squaliform sharks. The dataset comprises morphological data, i.e. dental characters, and nuclear exon sequences allowing the direct incorporation of fossil and extant taxa into the divergence time estimations. The Bayesian inference analysis results in a fully resolved phylogenetic tree, supporting the monophyly of the order Squaliformes. Most fossil taxa are clustering in accordance with their taxonomic allocation in previous studies. Somniosidae is paraphyletic in respect to Oxynotidae. New findings regarding the genus-level interrelationships of Somniosidae plead for a revision of the family. The phylogenetic placement and intrageneric relationships of the extinct genus Protospinax remain unclear. The extinct Paraphorosoides ursulae (†) clusters with Etmopteridae questioning its assignment to the Dalatiidae. Node ages estimated via fossil tip-dating are mostly resulting in older ages compared to previous estimates based on calibrated molecular clocks. We estimated the origin of Squaliformes to have occurred approx. 152 Ma ago. The occurrence of bioluminescence is dated to the Lower Cretaceous before the onset of the Cenomanian-Turonian global anoxic event. Thus, luminescent organs may have already been evolved before a re-colonisation of the deep sea after the crisis.

title: New data about vascularisation and histology in neoselachian teeth based on computed tomography
abstract_text: Based on their internal structure, elasmobranch teeth have been traditionally separated into two different dental histotypes, orthodond and osteodont. The orthodont histotype is characterised by teeth with an open pulp cavity surrounded by orthodentine and osteodentine, whereas in the osteodont histotype the pulp cavity is completely closed and teeth are formed only by osteodentine. However, this classification has recently been criticised because of its simplification (Moyer et al., 2015), existing species which teeth histology cannot be classified exactly within any of the classical described histotypes. To test and evaluate the variation of teeth histology within the Euselachii phylogeny, here we analysed teeth of several species of current elasmobranch using Synchrotron X-Ray Tomography Microscopy (SXRTM) to characterise their internal structure. The tridimensional reconstruction and the topographical analysis of the teeth have allowed us to identify the classic histotypes, but also describe other intermediate states, with teeth completely formed by orthodentine, or teeth with several dentine combinations in the cusp. These different arrangements could be explained by heterochronic processes affecting rates of the tissues within the teeth. Therefore, our results stand out the idea that the classical histotypes are a reductionist classification and don't reflect the real variation of this characters. The application of new methodologies, like microtomography with synchrotron, have demonstrated being a powerful tool for the study of the histology and the internal structures at submicrometric resolution.

title: Development and evolution of the cutting dentition of dogfish (squaliform) sharks

abstract_text: The dogfish (squaliform) sharks are dominant predators in many cool and deep seas. Most possess a unique dentition with teeth overlapping and locking together to form a continuous cutting blade on the jaw margin, either on both jaws or restricted to the lower jaw. This contrasts with the alternating pattern of teeth in almost all other sharks and rays. CT scanning of the developing teeth of the Spurdog Squalus acanthias and other squaliforms revealed that the first teeth in the embryo are arranged as in other sharks, realigning during growth to line up teeth from adjacent tooth rows. In species with more highly derived dentitions, the blade-like lower teeth first form in the embryo in a similar arrangement to in the adult of Squalus, wheres the small upper teeth retail their alternating pattern into adulthood. The possession of a unique cutting dentition allows squaliforms to feed on large food items (living or dead) when needed, giving them an evolutionary advantage in low nutrient or cold environments, where they have been focuses for their entire evolutionary history.

abstract_text: Nursery areas provide protection from predators and ample food supply for juvenile individuals of a species, the adults of which spend their lives in different habitats. The Rewa river Delta on Viti Levu, Fiji, has recently been identified as nursery area for the Scalloped Hammerhead Shark Sphyrna lewini. We evaluated the diet composition and the trophic position of neonate and young of the year (YOY) individuals within this nursery area. The information on the diet of the sharks will provide insight on whether the nursery area provides abundant food for the sharks. For this, a combination of stable isotope analysis of shark tissue and DNA-barcoding of gut contents was used. The analysis of the carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen composition (δ15N) of muscle tissue revealed a shift in the composition which correlated with the age of the juveniles. The maternal isotope signal was evident within the muscle tissue of neonates and fades as the sharks mature. The results of the DNA barcoding of the stomach content complement the study by identifying the preferred prey species.

abstract_text: Sharks and other polyphyodont vertebrates retain the crown gnathostome character of continuous successional regeneration of oral teeth. How capacity for successional regeneration is maintained in some lineages but lost from other (e.g. mammals) is currently unknown. We have shown that a compound and dynamic Sox2+ stem cell population resident in the shark dentition connects the superficial taste-competent oral epithelium at the taste/tooth-junction with the deep tooth-forming successional lamina via cells migrating through the lingual margin of the middle dental epithelium during successional regeneration of teeth. We have shown that both taste buds and teeth emerge from the odonto-gustatory band, a field of embryonic oral epithelium equivalent to the odonteogenic band of mammals, and that the Sox2+ stem niches of the taste/tooth-junction and the successional lamina are derived from the odonto-gustatory band. We provide evidence for the shark test-bite or taste-bite. We suggest that a novel collaboration between the generalized odontode gene regulatory network and the taste bud gene regulatory network specifically in the oropharynx was key to the evolutionary transformation between dermal odontodes (i.e. placoid scales) and oropharyngeal odontodes (i.e. teeth). Differential gene expression analyses preformed here with microdissected sub-regions of recently hatched shark dentition, including the taste/tooth-junction and successional lamina stem niches in addition to developing early teeth, erupting late teeth, and taste bud epithelium from the basihyal not associated with teeth offers novel insights into the molecular distinction between taste, tooth, and dual-competent epithelia via the discovery of shared and differentially expressed genes.
